analysis.one_liner: Bans the weedkiller atrazine, which contaminates farm-country water and drinking supplies.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban atrazine never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to use, make, sell, import, or export any pesticide containing atrazine, a widely used weedkiller. The bill's findings cite government data showing atrazine in roughly three-quarters of streams and 40 percent of groundwater samples in farm areas, measurable levels in more than 90 percent of samples from 139 drinking water systems, and links to reproductive harm in animals and humans. The European Union banned it in 2003. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water from farm country: the EPA's own monitoring found atrazine in most streams and groundwater in agricultural areas, and in drinking water systems across the Midwest and South. Farmworkers and rural residents exposed during spraying would also benefit, as would fish and amphibians, which the Fish and Wildlife Service says are harmed by atrazine.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans all use, production, sale, importation, and exportation of atrazine, eliminating the source of the contamination rather than capping it.

It cites EPA and USGS monitoring showing atrazine in about 75 percent of streams and 40 percent of groundwater samples in agricultural areas, and measurable levels in over 90 percent of samples from 139 drinking water systems.
It cites links between atrazine exposure and low sperm counts in men, low birth weight, and abnormal reproductive development in laboratory mammals and aquatic wildlife.
Violations would carry fines or up to two years in prison, giving the ban teeth.

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturer of atrazine and any distributors would lose their product entirely. Corn and other row-crop farmers would need substitutes; the USDA estimated a ban would cost only 1.19 percent of crop yield and reduce corn acreage by 2.3 percent, and Germany and Italy saw no drop in corn production after banning atrazine.
analysis.who_pays_short: Atrazine makers and some corn farmers

drawbacks.text: Farmers would lose a cheap, effective weedkiller; the Department of Agriculture estimated a ban would cause crop losses of 1.19 percent and cut corn acreage by 2.3 percent, a real if modest cost.

A single-chemical criminal ban, with prison terms of up to two years, overrides the EPA's normal pesticide review process rather than working through it, and applies immediately with no phase-in for stocks already in the supply chain.
Farmers would shift to other herbicides, whose own environmental effects the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental case is strong on the bill's own record: pervasive water contamination, documented reproductive harm, and a European ban already in place for years, all against a USDA-estimated crop cost of about one percent that Italy and Germany did not experience. The main honest objections are the abruptness of a full ban and the shift to substitute herbicides. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to four committees, then to two subcommittees, and none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on March 29, 2012, joined by Reps. Dennis Kucinich and James Moran as original cosponsors.
It was referred to four committees at once — Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Foreign Affairs — splitting jurisdiction and requiring any one of them to act.
Two subcommittee referrals followed within two weeks, and then nothing: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.
Ten Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did, and it never reached the floor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atrazine's manufacturer and the farmers who use it kept a product the bill would have banned, and the committees with jurisdiction faced no consequence for never acting. No one who drinks water from agricultural areas got the protection the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Atrazine's maker and its farm users

industries.industry: Atrazine manufacturers (led by Syngenta, the maker of the herbicide)
industries.note: Atrazine, used on 60 to 80 million pounds annually in the US, would be banned outright, wiping out the product's American sales. Its manufacturer profits from a chemical found in most farm-area water, so its interest runs directly against the water drinkers the bill protects.

Farmers would lose a cheap, effective weedkiller; the USDA put the cost at 1.19 percent of yield and a 2.3 percent cut in corn acreage, while noting Italy and Germany saw no production loss after their bans. Farm communities also bear the water contamination, so their interest cuts both ways.

industries.industry: Drinking water utilities in agricultural regions
industries.note: More than 90 percent of samples from 139 water systems had measurable atrazine, and utilities must test for and manage it; a ban removes the contaminant at its source.
